analysis.one_liner: Limits federal lawsuits over prison conditions and makes court-ordered releases for overcrowding nearly impossible.
analysis.headline: Introduced by the Senate Majority Leader with 13 cosponsors, the bill was sent to the Judiciary Committee the day it was filed and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would sharply cut back federal court oversight of prisons. It would let governments move to end existing court orders setting prison conditions, make court-ordered releases for overcrowding almost impossible to obtain, and require prisoners to pay filing fees, exhaust prison grievance systems, and meet higher bars to sue — including a ban on recovering for emotional injury without a physical injury and a bar on filing after three dismissed suits. The bill was sold as a curb on frivolous prisoner lawsuits; its larger effect would be to shield state and local corrections systems from lawsuits and judicially enforced reform.
analysis.who_benefits: State and local governments and their corrections agencies gain the most. Existing federal consent decrees and injunctions governing prison conditions would be terminable by any party two years after enactment — retroactively applying to orders already in force — and any new order must be the "least intrusive" fix for the specific plaintiffs before the court, with substantial weight given to public safety and prison-system impact. Prisoner-release orders for overcrowding would require a three-judge panel, prior failed less-intrusive orders, and findings by clear and convincing evidence. Corrections officials also gain from mandatory dismissal of claims that fail to state a case, caps on attorney fees, a waiver-of-reply option, and a bar on emotional-distress damages without physical injury. The stated public benefit is fewer frivolous filings and less judicial interference in running prisons.

how_it_helps.text: Lets any party seek termination of a federal court order governing prison conditions two years after it was granted — including orders issued before the bill — and requires courts to automatically suspend the order while a termination motion is pending

Caps every new court remedy at the narrowest fix for the specific plaintiffs, and requires judges to give substantial weight to any adverse impact on public safety or the operation of the criminal justice system

Makes prisoner-release orders for overcrowding nearly impossible: only a three-judge panel could issue one, only after less intrusive orders had failed, and only if it found by clear and convincing evidence that crowding was the primary cause and that no other relief would remedy it

Requires prisoners to exhaust available administrative grievance procedures before suing, and directs courts to dismiss suits on their own motion if the claim is frivolous, malicious, or fails to state a claim

Requires prisoners suing without prepayment to pay the full filing fee in installments from their prison accounts, bars anyone with three prior dismissed suits from filing again unless facing imminent danger of serious bodily harm, caps attorney fees at court-appointed counsel rates, and denies recovery for mental or emotional injury without a prior showing of physical injury

Requires the Attorney General to personally sign any Justice Department lawsuit, certification, or motion to intervene under the Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act, centralizing decisions to sue states over prison conditions

analysis.who_pays: Prisoners with genuine grievances bear the cost. They must exhaust grievance systems that the bill itself says states cannot be sued for failing to provide, pay filing fees they often cannot afford, and face dismissal screens at every stage. Attorneys who represent them face fee caps proportional to court-ordered relief, reducing the incentive to take valid cases. People held in unconstitutional or overcrowded facilities lose the main remedy courts have used — release or capacity orders — which the bill reserves for an almost unreachable standard. The public at large loses a check on how a government institution treats the people it holds.

drawbacks.text: The termination and least-intrusive rules apply retroactively to court orders already in force — including long-running consent decrees — so reform of prison systems under court supervision could be cut off two years after enactment even where conditions remained unconstitutional
When a defendant moves to terminate a court order, the order is automatically stayed while the motion is pending, meaning prisoners lose existing protections during the entire review period
The filing-fee requirement and the three-strikes bar apply to all prisoner suits, not just frivolous ones, so an indigent prisoner with a valid claim could be unable to get into court at all
Denying recovery for mental or emotional injury without a prior showing of physical injury would exclude real harms — such as prolonged isolation or threats — from any monetary remedy

By reserving release orders for a three-judge court applying a clear-and-convincing standard after less intrusive remedies have failed, the bill leaves almost no judicial path to remedy unconstitutional overcrowding, even when crowding itself causes the violation

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Cutting frivolous prisoner filings is a legitimate goal, and requiring prisoners to try a prison's grievance system first is defensible on its own. But the bill does not separate abusive cases from meritorious ones: the same machinery that screens out weak claims — fees, dismissal screens, fee caps, the physical-injury requirement, and retroactive termination of court orders — also forecloses valid claims and ends judicial oversight of prison conditions wholesale. For a bill whose stated purpose is procedural cleanup, the provisions aimed at legitimate claims and existing court orders are drastic, and the benefits flow overwhelmingly to the government entities being sued.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Judiciary Committee the same day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senate Majority Leader Bob Dole introduced the bill on September 27, 1995, joined by twelve Republican cosponsors and one Democrat, Senator Harry Reid of Nevada
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee that same day; no hearing, markup, or committee vote followed
The bill sat in committee until the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, and all legislative action on it ceased

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, prisoners kept the then-existing rules for suing in federal court without prepaying fees, and federal courts kept their full power to order remedies for unconstitutional prison conditions. State and local corrections systems did not get the new shields against lawsuits and court orders.

for.name: Bob Dole
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Prison Litigation Reform Act of 1995 and recruited an initial cosponsor slate

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a bipartisan face

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Received the referral; chaired by Sen. Orrin Hatch (R), who had cosponsored the bill
against.what_they_did: Held no hearing, markup, or vote and never reported the bill out; it died at referral when the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Twelve of the bill's thirteen cosponsors were Republicans; one Democrat, Harry Reid of Nevada, joined. No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split of any actual support beyond sponsorship is unknown.

industries.industry: State and local corrections agencies and governments
industries.note: The bill's core provisions — retroactive termination of consent decrees, near-impossible release orders, dismissal screens, and fee limits — all shift power from courts to the government entities being sued over prison conditions. Their gain is the removal of the main outside check on how they run their prisons.

industries.industry: Prison guards and corrections officers (and their unions)
industries.note: Suits over conditions and official conduct would face mandatory dismissal screens, fee caps, waiver-of-reply options, and a physical-injury prerequisite, making it much harder to hold individual officers accountable in court.

Attorney fees would be capped at court-appointed counsel rates, awarded only in proportion to court-ordered relief, and partially taken from the client's judgment, shrinking the economics of representing indigent prisoners.
